title: Improving Human-Generated Operational Data: Evidence from Pilot Competency Assessment
affiliations: , National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School, National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School and

detail.title: Improving Human-Generated Operational Data: Evidence from Pilot Competency Assessment
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly rely on data generated through human judgment to support operational decisions, yet the behavioral processes through which such data are produced can limit their usefulness. We study this issue in the context of pilot competency assessment at an international airline, where instructors evaluate pilots using a multi-level rating scale. Combining quantitative analysis with qualitative investigation, we first document substantial rating compression: instructors disproportionately assigned the midpoint of the rating scale across competency dimensions. Semi-structured interviews with experienced instructors provide qualitative evidence on the assessment practices underlying this pattern. Instructors report heterogeneous interpretations of the rating scale, reluctance to use extreme ratings, differences in the observability of competency dimensions, and time constraints that can make fine-grained assessment difficult. In collaboration with the airline, the training unit subsequently implemented an assessor workshop that used persona-based illustrations to clarify the intended interpretation and use of the rating scale. Using a multi-period difference-in-differences design with synthetic controls, we find that workshop participation increased within-instructor grading variation by approximately 25\%, consistent with reduced rating compression and greater differentiation in competency assessments. We further find that post-workshop ratings became more closely aligned with grading patterns predicted from historical assessments and observable trainee and training characteristics, although this evidence is less robust to alternative comparison-group definitions. Together, the findings show that an organizational intervention can change how human evaluators use an existing assessment scale and, in turn, the characteristics of the operational data they generate. More differentiated competency assessments may provide managers with more useful information for identifying training needs and tailoring subsequent training decisions.

title: The Half-Life of a Futures Contract: Technological Obsolescence and Vintage Risk in Compute Derivatives

detail.title: The Half-Life of a Futures Contract: Technological Obsolescence and Vintage Risk in Compute Derivatives
detail.abstract: A futures contract has a legal maturity, but it can lose economic relevance before that date. This paper develops the concept of contract half-life for derivatives written on rapidly evolving technological vintages. Contract half-life is the time required for a hardware-specific contract's economic relevancemeasured through commercial exposure, trading liquidity, and price-discovery importance-to fall to onehalf of its reference level. The distinction matters for compute derivatives because the announced H100 and B200 futures are tied to named GPU generations whose commercial importance can migrate faster than their rental prices disappear. A simple vintage-migration model separates rental-price depreciation from benchmark-relevance depreciation and shows how innovation intensity, maturity, and liquidity network effects jointly determine economic expiry. The model yields four testable propositions: activity should migrate to a new vintage faster than the old rental index declines; distant maturities of an oldvintage contract should lose viability first; faster innovation should shorten contract half-life; and rolling or performance-adjusted benchmarks should extend durability while increasing conversion-model and governance risk. The paper proposes observable half-life measures based on open interest, volume, information shares, and commercial benchmark adoption, and explains why a still-published settlement index is insufficient evidence that a contract remains economically alive. Because these propositions require post-launch data, the paper also uses three completed benchmark transitions-the shift of a gasoline contract to an RBOB basis, the ultra-low-sulfur respecification of heating oil, and the inclusion of WTI Midland in Dated Brent-plus unsuccessful DRAM-futures proposals as identification templates. These analogues distinguish benchmark replacement, internal respecification, constituent revision, and launch failure; they are not estimates or formal bounds on compute-contract half-life.

title: Familiarity, Trust and Diversification: Dual-Survey Evidence from Household Decision-Makers and Financial Advisors

detail.title: Familiarity, Trust and Diversification: Dual-Survey Evidence from Household Decision-Makers and Financial Advisors
detail.abstract: This study examines how familiarity, trust and perceived control are associated with household investment preferences, and whether financial advisors report comparable patterns. Two crosssectional convenience-sample surveys were analysed: 147 household respondents involved in financial decisions and 18 financial advisors or wealth professionals. Mutual funds were the most common comfortable destination for extra savings (46.2%, n = 143), while fixed deposits most often felt safest (39.3%, n = 140). Among 141 valid responses, 72.3% selected either a diversified financial mix or a combination of several assets as the ₹1 crore option that would help them sleep best. When the same ₹50 lakh was reframed as money earned slowly over many years, 28.9% said they would be more careful, compared with 6.3% who would be more willing to take risks. Tangible-asset comfort and belief that property or gold are safer were strongly associated (rs = .621, p < .001). Investment experience was associated with choosing a diversified option (χ²(2) = 17.14, p < .001). Advisors broadly corroborated the familiarity, trust and over-concentration patterns. The results suggest a familiarity-trust gap: many respondents supported diversification in principle, while willingness to act depended on credibility, family consultation and staged implementation.

title: Pricing Maritime Insecurity: Stock-Market Responses to Maritime Piracy
affiliations: University of Macedonia, , University of Macedonia - Department of Economics and Central Bank of Cyprus

detail.title: Pricing Maritime Insecurity: Stock-Market Responses to Maritime Piracy
detail.abstract: This study examines whether maritime piracy is priced at the level of the listed shipping firm connected to the affected vessel. We hand-collect incidents from the International Maritime Organization's monthly piracy and armed-robbery reports, match vessels to their owners or operators at the incident date and link the resulting exposures to daily equity returns. The rebuilt dataset contains 101 candidate event-security matches during 2014-2023; a security audit validates 97 of them. After excluding contaminated events or estimation windows and ownership links flagged for review, the primary sample comprises 55 incidents involving 29 listed firms. Event time is anchored to the first observed trading day on or after the incident. Expected returns are estimated over trading days-250 to-21 using a market model; Fama-French three-factor, Carhart four-factor and Fama-French fivefactor models provide robustness checks. Standard errors are clustered by ticker. On the common 54-event factorcalendar sample, the event-day average abnormal return ranges from-0.50% to-0.69%; it is significant under the market and Fama-French three-factor models, borderline under Carhart, and less precise under Fama-French fivefactor. In the primary market-model sample, the cumulative abnormal return over [0,+4] is-1.65% (p = 0.042). The negative response survives winsorization, pandemic-period exclusion and leave-one-firm-out checks, although precision beyond the event day is model-dependent. Exploratory regressions reveal no precisely estimated heterogeneity by vessel market, region, waters classification, reporting status or recorded loss. The evidence indicates that a localized maritime-security incident can generate a measurable firm-level valuation discount even when it need not move aggregate freight conditions.

The analysis traces publication growth, the leading journals and thematic clusters that ground the field, the dominant co-word structures linking AI capability, digital transformation, and firm performance, and the conceptual shift of AI from an operational efficiency tool toward a strategic organizational capability. The paper generalizes with a discussion of methodological limitations common to bibliometric work in these specific areas and proposes a future research agenda focus on longitudinal designs, better AI-capability measures, and underexplored contexts such as human-AI complementarity, SMEs and governance.

title: The Architecture of Alignment: How the Modern Republican Movement Built a Permanent Political System
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Architecture of Alignment: How the Modern Republican Movement Built a Permanent Political System
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the modern Republican movement is best understood not merely as a political party but as a functionally integrated political system linking donors, policy organizations, legal networks, media, religious institutions, campaigns, state governments, federal personnel, and voters. It examines the movement's development from permanent-campaign strategy through state-policy replication, REDMAP, census politics, judicial strategy, party discipline, election-fraud narratives, and the increasing institutional role of conservative religious authority. The paper distinguishes ordinary partisan competition from recursive political advantage: the use of temporary electoral power to alter the institutional conditions governing future political competition. It also examines bidirectional preference formation between political elites and voters, compares the Republican architecture with the differently organized Democratic coalition, and separates emergent system alignment from deliberate strategic conduct. The central claim is falsifiable: if the Republican ecosystem is genuinely integrated, policy, personnel, messaging, and institutional strategy should continue to move predictably across formally independent organizations. The paper concludes that the architecture becomes visible only when controversies usually treated as separate are examined as components of one political production system.

title: Progressive Taxation and Responsive Cost Sharing
affiliations: University of Amsterdam - Department of Quantitative Economics (KE)

detail.title: Progressive Taxation and Responsive Cost Sharing
detail.abstract: This paper provides a unified, axiomatic treatment of progressivity in two canonical distributive models: nonlinear income taxation and cost sharing of a joint technology. We compare rules using Lorenz-majorization of tax burdens and total cost-share vectors. In cost sharing, total cost shares are interpreted as demand-weighted unit-price burdens. For cost sharing we formalize progressivity as higher unit prices for larger demands under decreasing-returns (and the reverse under increasingreturns). Exploiting the isomorphism between monotonic rationing and additive cost sharing, we characterize classical rules by their progressive structure. The proportional rule is the unique self-dual boundary between progressivity and regressivity. Extremal ordered-priority constructions yield the most progressive and most regressive rules in the corresponding Lorenz order: the average ordered-priority rule is maximally progressive on convex technologies and maximally regressive on concave ones. Under a mild ranking axiom, the serial (leveling-based) rule attains maximal progressivity on convex domains (and the corresponding maximal regressivity on concave domains). The results clarify how technological curvature reverses the progressivity implications of cost-sharing rules.

title: Agile-Compliance Trade-Offs in Digitally Transformed Project Management: Balancing Flexibility and Regulatory Assurance
affiliations: MGIMO University

detail.title: Agile-Compliance Trade-Offs in Digitally Transformed Project Management: Balancing Flexibility and Regulatory Assurance
detail.abstract: Organizations operating in highly regulated, technology-intensive sectors face a persistent tension between the flexibility promised by agile project management methodologies and the procedural rigor demanded by quality and regulatory compliance frameworks. This paper develops a conceptual analysis of this tension, drawing on the author's master's research into digital transformation in project-based organizations. It examines how hybrid project management models-combining agile iteration with structured governance checkpoints-can reconcile rapid digital tool adoption with the documentation, traceability, and quality-assurance requirements typical of regulated industries. The paper further addresses cybersecurity as an emergent structural risk accompanying digital integration, arguing that data protection and system resilience must be embedded within project governance from the earliest stages rather than treated as a downstream compliance concern. The analysis concludes that organizations achieving durable digital maturity are those that institutionalize compliance-by-design principles within agile project structures rather than treating agility and regulation as opposing forces.

title: Automated Algorithm Selection for Integrated Healthcare Timetabling: Performance Prediction and Similarity Analysis
affiliations: Duke Kunshan University, Duke Kunshan University and Duke Kunshan University

detail.title: Automated Algorithm Selection for Integrated Healthcare Timetabling: Performance Prediction and Similarity Analysis
detail.abstract: Healthcare scheduling literature frequently addresses optimization problems in isolation.Due to ignoring the interdepencencies of those problems, there have been recent efforts in combining subsets of these problems such as integrating Patient Admission Scheduling (PAS) with Nurse-to-Patient Assignment (NPA). The Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Competition (IHTC) 2024 introduced a joint formulation, i.e. the Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Problem (IHTP), requiring the simultaneous optimization of 3 interdependent subproblems of PAS, NPA and Surgical Case Planning (SCP). The competition results revealed that no single competing algorithm dominates across the IHTP instances. To address this performance variability, this study presents the first application of Automated Algorithm Selection (AS) to the IHTP. Specifically, we develop rank-based performance prediction based AS models leveraging 5 hierarchically designed feature sets. By dynamically matching each instance with the algorithm with the highest predicted performance, 3 of those 5 AS models consistently outperform all the individual competing methods, including the competition winner, closing the gap toward the Virtual Best Solver (VBS) / Oracle. Beyond predictive accuracy, a similarity analysis is conducted across both algorithm and instance spaces using t-SNE clustering, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) and SHAP values. This analysis specify the critical structural features determining algorithms' performance variations. It is shown that derived operational features rather than raw instance cardinality features have been the leading identifiers for capturing algorithmic behavior, identifying the performance boundaries of each IHTP algorithm. The findings offer a reliable and systematic data-driven approach for optimizing complex healthcare optimization problems.

title: Khaki is the New Green. On Competition Law and EU's New Defence Posture

detail.abstract: The article examines the evolving relationship between EU competition law, Member States' prerogatives (in particular under Article 346 TFEU), and the Union's industrial policy in the defence sector. It does so against the backdrop of an explicit reorientation of the Commission's regulatory agenda, in which the green transition has given way to a notion of «defence readiness» that presupposes an equally far-reaching industrial reorganisation. Building on a review of case law, with a focus on concentrations, and enforcement practice, the article argues that the EU has thus far facilitated sector consolidation while at the same time seeking to establish reasonable limits on the exemption criterion that Member States may invoke for activities relating to their security. It also discusses definitional tensions in relation to dual-use products, special exceptions, and recent regulatory developments, including the Defence Readiness Omnibus and the ongoing revision of the Merger Guidelines. The conclusions underline how, notwithstanding recent expectations and declarations concerning industrial policy, both the existing legal frameworks and prevailing policy dynamics continue to anchor the integration of the defence industry in the prerogatives of the Member States. This occurs in a context in which the deterioration of longstanding geopolitical relationships and the Union's aspirations to strategic autonomy foreshadow developments that are as difficult as they are necessary, with plausible direct implications for EU competition law.

detail.abstract: Institutional writing, corporate memos, press releases, official statements, increasingly reads as if one system wrote all of it. This essay argues that large language models are a real cause of that sameness, not because anyone programmes them to write blandly, but because they are built to pick whichever words appear most often in similar writing, which is a mechanical way of avoiding anything unusual. Drawing on existing research into how institutions use language to hold onto power, on the organisational learning literature's account of why organisations protect their own blind spots, and on George Orwell's classic essay on political language, the essay argues that these systems remove the one thing that used to slow this drift down: a person, choosing their own words, occasionally choosing an honest one instead of a safe one. It then develops Learnable Theory's account of the linguistic exorcism (Magni, 2024): a noun-adjective pairing that installs a new orientation by suppressing a noun's own semantic field, and a five-step procedure for verifying, against three public criteria, when the suppressed content genuinely resists a frame's own logic rather than merely reflecting the analyst's projection. The essay checks this procedure against real evidence three times rather than asserting it: once by measuring how words relate to each other in meaning, once by measuring what an actual language model considers likely, reporting honestly that the two measurements disagree and using that disagreement to sharpen the argument rather than hide it, and once by actually prompting a real, smaller language model to generate exorcisms itself, reported as a preliminary observation rather than a settled result. The essay then runs the full procedure on its own opening sentence, and closes by asking what a language model can and cannot do with the test itself, arguing that the honest limit is narrower, and more interesting, than a flat impossibility.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relative identification and disclosure of sustainability-related Risks and Opportunities among European companies reporting under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) and the Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard for non-listed SMEs (VSME). It develops and applies a defined coding methodology to assess the balance between reported Risks and Opportunities across the research sample. The findings indicate a substantial asymmetry in the reporting of the two categories. The study examines the implications of this asymmetry for the interpretation of sustainability reporting and for the role of sustainability-related opportunity identification in corporate strategy. The research does not seek to establish the causal reasons for the observed asymmetry, but provides an empirical basis for further investigation.

title: Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing: Methodological Foundations *

detail.title: Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing: Methodological Foundations *
detail.abstract: Recent advances in LLM agents enable a new paradigm for asset pricing, which we call Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing (AEAP): systems that autonomously conduct the scientific discovery process itself. We define AEAP and identify its core building blocks. Existing evaluation practices backtest only the outputs—factors or trades—not the autonomous discovery system that produced them. We focus on factor discovery, contributing a reference architecture, a rigorous evaluation standard for discovered factors, and a method for out-of-sample backtesting the discovery system. As a concrete instance of that architecture, we evaluate SEADS against five re-implemented baselines on two US equity panels using this standard: no single metric ranks the systems consistently, motivating evaluation on multiple axes at once. A separate rolling re-execution then asks the complementary question of whether the discovery process itself, not one static output, is reliable. We also report negative findings and limitations that surface further evaluation pitfalls for future AEAP systems.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the United States' federal statutory framework for gender equity in employment, the Equal Pay Act (1963), Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (1964), the Pregnancy Discrimination Act (1978), the Family and Medical Leave Act (1993), and the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act (2009), as a potential comparator for reforming HR practice and policy in Nigeria's formal manufacturing sector. It deliberately excludes voluntary, non-statutory corporate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programming from the comparator model, because such programming is presently being dismantled at the US federal level: executive orders issued in January 2025 and March 2026 eliminated federal DEI offices, ended affirmative-action obligations for federal contractors, and directed the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and Department of Justice to treat many DEI initiatives as potentially unlawful under Title VII. This rollback is itself treated as evidence in the analysis: an instructive illustration that voluntary, non-legislated equity programming is politically reversible in a way that binding statutory floors are not. Drawing on Nigerian labour-market data, the paper documents that women's severe underrepresentation in Nigeria is concentrated specifically in formal-sector supervisory and senior-management job titles, not in the broader, informally-dominated "manager" category in which Nigeria in fact ranks among the world's highest for female representation, a distinction essential to accurately diagnosing the problem. This paper proposes an institutional transferability framework and argues on the strength of the 2025-2026 US experience, that Nigeria should prioritise binding legislative and regulatory floors over voluntary corporate commitments when adapting foreign HR equity models.

detail.abstract:
Volume II in the series Concentrated Benefit, Dispersed Burden. 264 pages, fifteen chapters in five parts, six appendices.


The Tennessee Valley Authority builds transmission lines across seven states and files no siting case for any of them. No state or federal body issues a certificate, holds a hearing on need, or reviews the route. The General Accounting Office reported the condition to Congress in 1982 - "the TVA Act does not require public involvement or information programs" - listed statutory fixes, and neither was enacted. Because nothing requires TVA to publish, what it chooses to publish is the public record.


This volume measures that record. Eighteen Tennessee transmission project pages are coded field by field: sixteen stated purposes name neither an end-use customer nor a load type, no page anywhere states a megawatt figure, and the environmental-review section is identical across all eighteen. From TVA's own published route geometry, the volume computes that TVA studies 2.63 miles of corridor for every mile it selects. It reconstructs the categorical-exclusion record from 11,899 published determinations, and shows that exclusion 16's 125-acre right-of-way cap binds before its ten-mile figure for any corridor wider than about 103 feet.


Two tests changed the argument and both are reported against the author. Eighteen Dominion Energy Virginia project pages, coded against the same three codes, name an end-use customer on none of eighteen, and Dominion files a full adversary certificate case at the State Corporation Commission. The utility with the forum names fewer customers than the utility without one, so the claim that a missing forum produces a missing name does not survive and is withdrawn. What the forum produces is a pointer: fourteen of eighteen Dominion pages carry an SCC case number. TVA has nowhere to point. Separately, a search of independent public records established that only three of the eighteen Tennessee projects had a nameable end-use customer at all, so the general practice claim an earlier draft made is withdrawn for want of a denominator.


The evidence is deposited separately and by hash at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21959989. The volume itself is at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21996376. The records-request handbook is published separately as Getting the Record.

title: WP -003 Closing the Loop: Circular Infrastructure and Nigeria's Resource Economy

detail.title: WP -003 Closing the Loop: Circular Infrastructure and Nigeria's Resource Economy
detail.abstract: Nigeria generates approximately 30 to 32 million tonnes of municipal solid waste annually. Less than 10 percent is recovered for productive reuse. Meanwhile, Nigerian manufacturers import the polymer feedstocks, secondary metals, and paper fibre that exist as waste in the same urban economy. The gap between what industry demands and what the waste system recovers is not an environmental statistic. It is a structural economic cost. This paper argues that circular infrastructure — the physical systems that collect, sort, process, and redirect secondary materials back into productive use — is the missing layer in Nigeria's industrial economy. It proposes a network of Circular Resource Hubs integrating collection, sorting, processing, and market linkage in coordinated regional facilities, designed to work with existing informal recovery networks rather than displace them. Drawing on precedents from China, South Africa, and Morocco, and grounded in Nigerian case examples across Lagos, the Niger Delta, and agro-industrial corridors, the paper sets out a practical implementation framework and financing model. The policy implication is direct: circular economy strategy in Nigeria must shift from environmental compliance to industrial infrastructure investment.

detail.title: From Paper Mill to Papermiller: Semantic Expansion, Evidentiary Escalation and Person-Level Labelling in Research-Integrity Commentary
detail.abstract: The term paper mill has become prominent in research-integrity discourse, but its public use is not confined to descriptions of commercial or organised manuscript-production operations. In some commentary, the same lexical root is extended to publications, researchers, collaborators, laboratories, journals, service providers and professional relationships through expressions such as papermiller, papermilling, papermill fraud, papermill dealer, papermill associate and papermill-infested. This article examines whether that semantic expansion is accompanied by an equally visible escalation in evidence. A structured qualitative content analysis was conducted using the 14 August 2026 edition of Schneider Shorts on For Better Science, a journalism and commentary website, as the focal corpus, supplemented by selected public material and formal paper-mill guidance. The analysis distinguishes observable anomaly, recognised paper-mill indicator, convergent suspicion, direct provenance evidence, individual knowing participation and identity-level attribution. Under the stated counting rules, the focal article contains 44 visible occurrences of paper-mill terminology or derivatives when embedded and quoted uses are included; a normalised manual count leaves approximately 38 occurrences in the running editorial text. More important than frequency is semantic range: the terminology is repeatedly attached to people, relationships, laboratories, journals and service providers, not only to manuscript-production organisations. The analysis identifies examples in which the publicly displayed evidence establishes a retraction, authorship irregularity, suspicious figure, external analytical service, editorial-process breach or other reason for investigation, while the textual step establishing commercial paper-mill provenance or knowing individual participation is not made explicit. By contrast, STM's paper-mill detection infrastructure describes signals and indicators as triggers for investigation rather than automatic findings. The article develops the concepts of paper-mill semantic expansion and evidentiary escalation and proposes a terminology protocol requiring increasingly severe public labels to be supported by increasingly specific and person-level evidence. The argument is not that strong terminology should be prohibited; it is that a noun should not silently perform evidentiary work that the evidence itself has not performed.

detail.abstract: We develop a contextualized large language model (LLM) framework that converts firm-specific news into auditable, industry-aware ESG narrative signals for S&P 500 firms. Anchoring prompts in the GICS hierarchy and SASB materiality standards, the two-stage pipeline separates semantic extraction from quantitative scoring and enforces point-intime discipline. Narrative sentiment predicts cumulative abnormal returns over 11-and 21-day event windows, and the market response strengthens sharply with the model's evidentiary confidence, consistent with gradual diffusion of unstructured sustainability information. Decomposing by pillar, governance events drive the unconditional drift, whereas environmental narratives are weakly or negatively priced on average. This apparent irrelevance is conditional: after a salient negative governance event, environmental news is strongly rewarded as evidence of remediation and legitimacy repair, while governance-quiet firms see environmental claims discounted as cost commitments. Governance credibility thus determines whether corporate environmental communication is priced as value creation.

detail.abstract: Child marriage remains a significant social and developmental concern in India, with women's education being an important factor associated with marriage timing. This study examines the relationship between women's schooling and child marriage prevalence across 707 districts using district-level data from the NFHS-5, 2019-2021. Women's schooling is measured as proportion of women aged 15-49 years with 10 or more years of schooling, while child marriage is measured as proportion of women aged 20-24 years married before age 18. Using Pearson's product-moment correlation and OLS regression, the study finds a statistically significant negative association between the two variables. The Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient of-0.6521 indicates a strong negative relationship. The regression results further show that a one percentage point increase in the proportion of women with 10+ years of schooling is associated with a 0.573 percentage point decrease in child marriage prevalence, with the model explaining approximately 42.5% of cross-district variation. While the cross-sectional design does not permit causal inference, the findings highlight the importance of women's schooling in addressing child marriage and support policies aimed at improving girls' access to and continuation in secondary education.

detail.abstract: This article examines the emergence and institutional diversity of Islamic higher education in Europe and develops a comparative typology of its principal institutional models. While existing scholarship has focused primarily on individual countries, institutions, or debates concerning imam training, a systematic comparative framework for understanding the broader landscape of Islamic higher education remains underdeveloped. Using a comparative institutional analysis of developments in the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, Austria, England, France, Spain, and Italy, the study examines historical trajectories, state–religion relations, institutional structures, accreditation systems, leadership formation, and sources of legitimacy. The findings demonstrate that Islamic higher education in Europe has not developed through a single institutional pathway. Instead, five ideal-type models can be identified: the Independent Islamic University Model, the State-Integrated Islamic Theology Model, the Seminary-Based Model, the Hybrid Partnership Model, and the Emerging and Transitional Model. The study contributes to the literature by providing a comparative framework for analyzing institutional diversity and by proposing a typology that facilitates future research on Islamic higher education, Muslim institutionalization, and religious leadership in Europe.

title: Authority Without Audit: Elisabeth Bik, the Missing Reproducibility Record, and the Governance Failure of Scientific Sleuthing
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: Authority Without Audit: Elisabeth Bik, the Missing Reproducibility Record, and the Governance Failure of Scientific Sleuthing
detail.abstract: Elisabeth Bik has become one of the most visible actors in post-publication image scrutiny. This article tests the scientific and institutional basis of that authority rather than accepting reputation, awards or correction counts as validation. A document-based audit identifies a consequential reproducibility defect in the 2016 mBio study that made the 'one in 25' formulation famous: the official code calls multiple external input files absent from the public supplements, while the available spreadsheet reports aggregate journal-by-year totals rather than the paper-level record of 20,621 screening decisions. The corpus was assembled through journal-site searches, often using the first 40–50 displayed results, and was dominated by one journal. Initial screening was performed by one person; coauthor review was limited to candidate positives; supplementary figures were searched asymmetrically; and the false-negative rate remains unknown. Counts also move from 782 to 781 and from 348 to 347 and 346 across code and derivative analysis without a public reconciliation. These defects do not prove fabrication, but they prevent independent replication and materially limit generalisation. The later record adds a governance problem: paid confidential consultancy, speaking income, an ethics-committee stipend, free forensic tools, crowdfunding, an independently directed fund within the parent of Retraction Watch, public accusations and media amplification coexist without a public case-level conflict and recusal registry. The evidence does not establish secret coordination, corrupt motive, platform capture or involvement in the uBiome founders' alleged conduct. It establishes a narrower but serious conclusion: Bik's alerts should be treated as leads, not findings; her prevalence figure should not be presented as a population estimate; and institutions should withhold presumptive expert or adjudicative status until methods, data lineage, conflicts, validation and correction symmetry are independently auditable.

detail.title: Asset Manager Capture

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 957/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
One of the most significant corporate governance developments of the past half-century is the rise of asset managers with large ownership stakes that provide them with outsized influence over public companies. As asset managers have grown in size, concerns about their potential to capture the government and secure favorable regulation have increased as well. In this Article, however, we describe an equally important risk that runs in the other direction: large asset managers are vulnerable to “reverse capture,” whereby government actors can pressure them to deploy their governance power in service of the government’s agenda.

This dynamic has intensified as presidential power has expanded over several decades. Expanded presidential authority not only enables administrations to bypass legislative and independent agency processes for regulating asset managers but also allows the White House to harness asset managers’ quasi-regulatory power to promote its agenda. These dynamics have implications not only for U.S. corporate governance and asset manager fiduciary duties, but also for global investors who rely on American asset managers. They also pose a democratic concern: government actors may increasingly pursue policy through concentrated private intermediaries rather than through more transparent and accountable channels.

title: Emerging Geopolitical Alliances or Issue-Specific Coalitions? A Network Analysis of UN General Assembly Voting Patterns (2016-2025)

detail.title: Emerging Geopolitical Alliances or Issue-Specific Coalitions? A Network Analysis of UN General Assembly Voting Patterns (2016-2025)
detail.abstract: This study examines whether voting alignment in the United Nations General Assembly reflects fixed geopolitical alliances or issue-specific coalitions that shift depending on the resolution at hand. Using roll-call voting records from Sessions 71 to 79 (2016-2025), the analysis applies social network analysis and the Louvain community detection algorithm to four voting networks: an aggregate network covering all resolutions, and three issue-specific networks addressing Russia-Ukraine, Gaza and Palestine, and Climate and Development resolutions. Pairwise voting agreement scores were calculated for every pair of states, and links below a 0.70 threshold were removed before community detection was applied. The Aggregate network produced a recognizable but weakly separated division, below the 0.3 reference threshold. Ukraine produced by far the strongest community structure, well above threshold, while Gaza showed broad consensus and weak bloc formation, with Climate and Development falling between the two. Among the G4, Germany and Japan clustered together throughout, while India and Brazil converged on Aggregate and Climate votes but split on Ukraine and Gaza. Shared institutional goals do not translate into stable voting cohesion; UNGA politics are better described through issue-specific coalitions than fixed geopolitical alliances.

title: Bounding Neighborhood Opportunity Loss for Housing Choice Voucher Tenants from Landlord Discrimination: A Counterfactual Rent Gap Approach
affiliations: and University of Washington - College of Built Environments

detail.title: Bounding Neighborhood Opportunity Loss for Housing Choice Voucher Tenants from Landlord Discrimination: A Counterfactual Rent Gap Approach
detail.abstract: While the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program aims to enable lowincome households to access high-opportunity neighborhoods, landlord discrimination in the private rental market systematically impedes such upward mobility. Using 2015-2023 American Housing Survey data across 15 MSAs, this study develops the empirical concept of the counterfactual rent gap to measure the cost of landlord discrimination. Through propensity score matching, we find that HCV tenants pay an average of 46.07% less in out-of-pocket rent than similar unsubsidized market renters. Through a bounding framework leveraging leaser-in-place HCV tenants and top-income tenants under Small Area Fair Market Rents (SAFMR), we isolate the neighborhood opportunity loss within the range of 23.48% to 45.65%, which accounts for 51.0% to 99.1% of the rent gap. Furthermore, our policy evaluation shows no significant effects of source of income (SOI) nondiscrimination protection laws on the neighborhood opportunity loss, which is likely due to weak enforcement. Meanwhile, SAFMR yields heterogeneous outcomes, effectively narrowing neighborhood opportunity loss in slack housing markets while widening the loss in tight markets. Policymakers should therefore prioritize proactive enforcement of SOI laws, the reduction of administrative burdens, and subsidy designs tailored to local market contexts.

title: Visibility-Based Performance Appraisal and Corporate
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Visibility-Based Performance Appraisal and Corporate
detail.abstract: The paper looks at the problem of performance evaluation when assessment is based on visibility rather than on the worker's actual productive effort. It examines an organization that has three levels: management, a manager, and the workers. The compensation of both the manager and the workers consists of fixed wages together with bonuses, while the management's remuneration is the firm's profit. Since both the manager and the workers do not bear the full risk associated with the firm's performance, there is an incentive for them to shirk their efforts when performance is evaluated on the basis of visibility. In the case of full observation-that is, when both the manager's and the workers' effort can be observed-the paper demonstrates that the target is achieved through genuine productive effort. However, under a system that relies on visibility, workers can combine their productive effort with artificial-visibility effort such as self-promotion, networking, and face time, etc. The model shows that the use of artificial-visibility efforts reduces both productive effort and residual corporate profit, while at the same time lowering the worker's private cost of earning the bonus. When there is a fixed production target, the effort put into making genuine work more visible is non-monotonic, meaning that productive effort first increases and then decreases as genuine effort becomes more effective in meeting the set target. The model then introduces an ex post collusion stage at which a worker can pay the manager to inflate an otherwise inadequate score. Collusion takes place only when the worker's cost savings from managerial manipulation are greater than the amount that the manager requires as compensation, which means that a larger share of the managerial profit and a higher manipulation cost can prevent collusion. Finally, the paper separates residual corporate profit from total organizational surplus and shows that the order in which the different evaluation systems rank these two measures does not have to be the same. The paper presents a unified threshold-bonus framework that brings together imperfect performance measurement, impression-management effort, and ex post managerial collusion, thereby providing new comparative-static insights into worker incentives and organizational performance.

detail.abstract:
This article asks whether Turkey could become a “new Iran,” not by reproducing Iran’s clerical institutions, Shi‘i ideology, Revolutionary Guard structure, or proxy network, but by assuming some of the regional security and threat functions historically associated with post-1979 Iran through a different ideological and institutional form. Beginning with the late nineteenth-century sovereignty crises of the Ottoman and Qajar states, the article traces how two powerful regional actors developed different state-building logics while operating within asymmetric international environments described here as hegemonic corridors.

The comparison is developmental rather than static. Instead of equating the mature Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) with the Gülen movement, the article compares the formative stages of Khomeini-centered religious organization under the Shah with the development of the Gülen network in Turkey: charismatic religious authority, intermediary cadres, educational institutions, merchant and business support, donation-based resource mobilization, alternative loyalties, and gradual penetration of formal institutions. In Iran, this process became state-founding after 1979 and eventually produced a constitutionalized Supreme Leader–IRGC order. In Turkey, the Gülen network and the Justice and Development Party (AKP) initially functioned as two complementary Islamist-derived centers in weakening the old military-bureaucratic tutelage before becoming rival projects of sovereignty.

The article interprets the 2013–2016 struggle and the failed coup of 15 July 2016 as a conflictual institutional succession through which the Gülen-centered pole was destroyed while political, administrative, and security power became increasingly concentrated in an AKP-centered, Reis-led party-state. The article does not argue that Turkey and Iran are converging toward the same regime type. Its central question is functional and conditional: as Iran’s half-century revolutionary-security order approaches either exhaustion or transformation, will Turkey institutionalize its own recent regime-security intensification and reproduce some of the same regional functions through a different Sunni-conservative, nationalist, Ottomanist, and state-centric ideological carrier?

The modern history of Turkey and Iran is therefore read neither as permanent rivalry nor as continuous external design, but as the history of powerful local actors producing different logics of state formation at different historical moments within hegemonic corridors.

detail.abstract: In this paper, Ralf Poscher addresses the question of what substantive freedom or interest the right to data protection is about. Drawing on German and European judgments on data protection and on theoretical conceptualizations of privacy, the author argues that data protection does not safeguard against actual violations (or at least a concrete danger of violation) of a particular liberty or interest, as fundamental rights usually do. Rather, data protection is concerned with potential and abstract dangers associated with the use of personal data that may lead to the violation of other fundamental rights, such as freedom of association or freedom of expression. On this basis, the author puts forward the thesis that the right to data protection is a preventive enhancement of other constitutionally guaranteed rights and freedoms. The adoption of such a conception of data protection leads to a more systematic approach than the one currently prevailing in Germany and Europe. This new perspective focuses not only on the collection of personal data, but takes into account the entire data processing system and its context.

detail.title: The Macroeconomics of Trade Wars: Tariffs, Retaliation, and Reallocation of Global Value Chains
detail.abstract: We study how tariffs affect sectors and countries globally, developing a multi-country model with 30 OECD economies, 62 industries, heterogeneous firms, and endogenous trade reallocation. Unilateral tariffs generate stagflation in imposing economies but contraction with disinflation in targeted ones. Sectoral prices depend on tariff exposure and reallocation capacity: cost-push inflation where inputs are hard to replace, demand-pull deflation where sales cannot be redirected. Retaliation redistributes rather than eliminates costs; delay compounds them. Under 2025 "Liberation Day" tariffs and reciprocal retaliation, trade contracts and U.S. centrality declines; Europe and the Rest of the World gain, leaving a smaller, more multipolar network.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a regime object-construction framework for interpreting football-linked market environments under bounded archival conditions. In this paper, "market" refers to an explicitly defined football-linked information environment rather than a financial market mechanism. A football-linked market regime is treated not as a latent state to be estimated or a portable condition to be forecast, but as a bounded research object fixed by a stated competition, season and historical envelope. "Regime" therefore functions as a research object rather than a predictive state variable; its description relates competition-phase context to pre-event observation boundaries. The framework addresses a recurring problem in football research: public records can become larger while the conditions that give those records meaning become less visible. A shared competition family, a repeated match count or a common model structure can make unlike environments appear interchangeable. Fixtures, results, tables, datasets and recurring patterns each have a legitimate role, but none automatically provides the full structural context in which observations were made. The contribution is a synthesis of those materials into an object-construction method that preserves archival continuity, boundary discipline, dual temporal axes and governed descriptive interpretation. The paper distinguishes this approach from predictive regime-switching methods, in which a regime is commonly an estimated state, and identifies a path for empirical evaluation of the public protocol.

title: Local Governance and Maternal Health Outcomes: A Case Study of Nepal's Decentralized Health Reforms

detail.title: Local Governance and Maternal Health Outcomes: A Case Study of Nepal's Decentralized Health Reforms
detail.abstract: Nepal has made impressive gains in reducing maternal deaths in the last 25 years. The maternal mortality ratio dropped from 539 to 151 deaths per 100,000 live births between 1996 and 2022. During the same period, skilled birth attendance rose from 9% to 77% and institutional delivery from 8% to 79%. Alongside these improvements have been major reforms in the health system, especially decentralization. The Local Self-Governance Act of 1999 assigned local bodies responsibility for health facilities. In 2015, the Constitution of Nepal established a federal system with 753 local governments responsible for basic health services. This case study explores the role of decentralization in improving maternal health outcomes in Nepal. It draws on data from national demographic and health surveys, policy documents, and global health estimates. The study finds that decentralization was helpful as it increased local resources, improved community participation, strengthened accountability, and supported national programs such as the Aama Program.

title: Ontology as the Semantic Foundation of Enterprise AI An Enterprise Semantic Architecture for Manufacturing Intelligence through a Comprehensive Review, Conceptual Framework, and Future Research Agenda

detail.title: Ontology as the Semantic Foundation of Enterprise AI An Enterprise Semantic Architecture for Manufacturing Intelligence through a Comprehensive Review, Conceptual Framework, and Future Research Agenda
detail.abstract:
The diffusion of large language models (LLMs) and generative artificial
intelligence (AI) into enterprise and industrial settings has renewed, rather
than resolved, the case for formal ontology. Statistical language models
exhibit well-documented failure modes, including factual hallucination and
unstable reasoning over long-tail and temporal facts, that are structurally
difficult to eliminate through scale alone [1,2]. Manufacturing enterprises,
meanwhile, continue to operate fragmented data landscapes spanning
Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), Manufacturing Execution Systems
(MES), Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA), and Industrial
Internet of Things (IIoT) platforms, in which syntactic connectivity has
outpaced semantic interoperability [3,4]. This paper develops an integrative,
critical review of ontology as the semantic substrate connecting knowledge
representation, knowledge graphs, neuro-symbolic and composite AI,
retrieval-augmented generation, agentic AI, business intelligence (BI), and
digital twins in manufacturing enterprises. Rather than treating these as
parallel literatures, the paper synthesises them around a single argument:
ontology is the layer that converts heterogeneous, syntactically interoperable
data into a shared, machine-interpretable conceptualisation capable of
supporting explainable inference, auditability, and cross-system reasoning
that neither conventional databases nor purely statistical models can provide
alone [5,6]. Drawing on the standards landscape, including the Asset
Administration Shell (AAS), RAMI 4.0, ISO 23247, ISA-95, OPC UA information
models, and W3C Semantic Web standards (RDF, RDFS, OWL, SPARQL, SKOS),
the paper critically compares ontology against adjacent constructs
(taxonomy, data model, metadata, knowledge graph) and against emergent AI
paradigms (LLMs, graph neural networks, agentic multi-agent systems). It
proposes a seven-layer Enterprise Semantic Architecture tracing the path
from raw enterprise data through semantic integration, ontology, knowledge
graph, reasoning, business rules, hybrid AI models, and agentic decision-
making to manufacturing and decision intelligence outcomes, illustrated
through a manufacturing case study spanning quality, maintenance, energy,
and supply-chain decision-making. The review identifies persistent research
gaps around ontology-LLM co-design, scalable reasoning over industrial-scale
knowledge graphs, and the governance of hybrid neuro-symbolic pipelines,
and closes with a future research agenda and managerial, industrial, and
policy implications.

title: Conversational AI for Frontline Educators: Evidence from a Large-Scale Deployment in India
affiliations: Rocket Learning, Rocket Learning, Rocket Learning and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Conversational AI for Frontline Educators: Evidence from a Large-Scale Deployment in India
detail.abstract: India operates nearly 1.4 million Anganwadi centerscommunity-based childcare and preschool centers providing free education, nutrition, and health services that are especially important to low-income households. Their educators combine classroom instruction with reporting and publicservice responsibilities. They often make situated decisions with limited time, incomplete observations, and delayed pedagogical guidance. We present and evaluate Shiksha Saathi, a conversational generative AI assistant designed for this setting. The Hindi-language assistant, developed and deployed by Rocket Learning, was delivered through WhatsApp to support more than 9,000 Anganwadi educators across 18 districts in Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. It was designed to address two recurring bottlenecks in frontline educational work: Guided Journalling turns brief classroom observations into weekly reports and recommendations, while Knowledge Assistance answers immediate questions using approved curricula. We follow the deployment across four versions and evaluate the mature service using longitudinal Guided Journalling records, human review of both pathways, and a survey of 152 educators. The Guided Journalling records show new reach, returning use, and recurring reporting near the intended cadence. Human review finds that the structured journalling pathway generally preserved consequential information through the persistent record. Open-ended assistance usually produced actionable responses, but its grounding and retrieval quality were less consistent. These findings show why conversational AI for frontline work must be designed as a technical and organizational service. They also suggest that specificity and persistence should increase only with information reliability.

title: Who may Open the Door? Access as the Key for Constitutional Jurisdictions to Defend Constitutional Justice
affiliations: and University of Hamburg - Faculty Of Law

detail.title: Who may Open the Door? Access as the Key for Constitutional Jurisdictions to Defend Constitutional Justice
detail.abstract: Access rules for constitutional review determine the institutional role constitutional actors perform within a constitutional order. This article argues that access to constitutional review is a multidimensional and gradable concept that better captures the opportunities for defense of constitutional justice recognized to constitutional jurisdictions than the classical American/European dichotomy. It proposes to replace traditional models of constitutional justice with a relational model of constitutional jurisdictions as the principal framework for comparative constitutional law.

title: Manufacturing Robots and their Short-term Demand for Energy: Evidence from OECD Countries

detail.title: Manufacturing Robots and their Short-term Demand for Energy: Evidence from OECD Countries
detail.abstract: The manufacturing sector is a major contributor to global energy consumption. Using a Translog Variable Cost Function approach, this study investigates the short-term energy demand effects of industrial robot adoption in manufacturing. By constructing a quality-adjusted robot stock and restricting the sample to industries with meaningful exposure to robot adoption, the analysis reduces the risk of overstating the energy-efficiency effects embedded in automation technologies. Based on a panel of 11 OECD countries, 9 manufacturing industries, and 13 years, I find a statistically significant but modest negative energy demand elasticity of-0.019%. This indicates that robots substitute for energy in the short term and reduce energy's share in variable costs. The estimated effect is substantially smaller than that of Information and Communication Technology (ICT), measured consistently within the same empirical framework and data setting. Further analysis shows that, despite their limited effect on total energy demand, robots may contribute to the greening of manufacturing by reducing the share of fossil fuels in the energy mix while leaving electricity demand unaffected. These findings have two main policy implications. First, industrial robots can contribute to less energy-intensive manufacturing and should therefore be considered in policies addressing the interaction between the digital and green transformations. At the same time, their environmental contribution should not be overstated. Second, debates on robot taxation aimed at mitigating adverse labor-market effects should also account for the potential sustainability benefits of robotization. Alternative policy responses, including worker retraining, innovation incentives, and targeted subsidies, may help address labor-market concerns while preserving the environmental benefits of automation.

title: Dethroning the event: where the harm really lies — recognition, regulatory flexibility, and the social production of post-traumatic outcomes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dethroning the event: where the harm really lies — recognition, regulatory flexibility, and the social production of post-traumatic outcomes
detail.abstract: Why does a potentially traumatic event leave one person functionally unharmed and another with a chronic, disabling disorder? This position paper argues that the dominant, event-centred model of psychological injury—in which the magnitude of the stressor is expected to predict the severity of the harm—is empirically untenable, and that the heterogeneity of outcome is better explained by processes that lie outside the event. Drawing together five research traditions that converge on this conclusion from incompatible methodological directions—Young's genealogy of the psychiatric apparatus, Fassin and Rechtman's moral economy of victimhood, Das's phenomenology of acknowledgment, Simpson's account of idioms of distress, and Bonanno's empirical science of resilience—the paper advances the recognition–flexibility hypothesis: that regulatory flexibility is necessary but not sufficient for recovery, and that its protective effect is conditioned by the relational and institutional field that recognises or withholds the legitimacy of a person's distress. The argument is illustrated through five hypothetical cases of Australian police officers, constructed as a quasi-controlled series in which the event is held constant while the field of recognition and the individual's capacity are varied. The paper develops implications for clinical practice, mental health services, and compensation systems, and meets the principal objections to the thesis directly, including the dose-response evidence and the risk of dissolving responsibility. It closes by specifying the conditions under which the reframing must not be over-extended: dethroning the event is not abolishing it, and the account is causal and developmental, never a means of blaming the injured or exculpating those who do harm.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the role of the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) Kenya as a disruptive infrastructure intervention and its influence on modal shift dynamics within the country's transport system, with particular focus on the Mombasa-Nairobi corridor. The study seeks to find out the impact of the SGR on the shift of freight and passenger transport from road to rail, examine the influence of transport cost, travel time, reliability, and safety on modal choice, and assess its effects on profitability, employment, and service coverage within the road freight and bus transport sectors. It also explores the perceptions and experiences of key transport stakeholders, including truck drivers, transport investors, clearing and forwarding employees, shippers, commuters, and regulators, concerning the disruptive effects of the SGR. Accordingly, the study will use deductive reasoning, positivism and an objectivist/realist orientation primarily for the quantitative strand, while inductive reasoning, subjectivism and interpretivism will primarily guide the qualitative strand. Ontology and epistemology will underpin both strands, although their application will differ according to the type of knowledge being generated. This philosophical arrangement is consistent with the convergent mixedmethods design and its objective of integrating statistical evidence with stakeholder experiences to understand the disruptive dynamics of the SGR in Kenya. The study will make use of a convergent mixed-methods research design, that will use both quantitative and qualitative research methods. Quantitative data will be gathered through structured face-to-face questionnaires using stratified random sampling, whereas qualitative data will be gathered using semi-structured interviews with purposively selected information-rich participants. Quantitative data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square tests, correlation, confidence intervals, and multiple linear regression, while qualitative data will be analyzed thematically. Triangulation will be used to merge the qualitative and quantitative data analysed at the interpretation stage. This study is expected to provide an all-inclusive intel of the financial, management, and community consequences of SGR-induced modal shifts and generate evidence-based policy recommendations for promoting an efficient, competitive, balanced, and sustainable multimodal transport system in Kenya.

detail.abstract: The study is concerned with the effectiveness of employing volunteer reserve defense force cadets in law enforcement. The study investigates whether the skills required for an law enforcement career are fostered by cadet training. 23 individual attributes essential for policing, grouped into five categories, were assessed among 321 cadets through two stages: a survey of 302 cadets and interviews with 19. Furthermore, 9 Ex-cadet police officers were interviewed to verify the advantages cadet training provided them compared to their non-cadet peers. Overall, the skills beneficial to law enforcement i.e. discipline, leadership, emergency response, commitment, etc. were reported significantly high among cadets. Cadets also scored high on public engagement and trust due to the nature of their duties. BNCC duties also frequently require cadets to assist law enforcement, which provides them with hands-on training of policework. The findings show that pipeline programs from BNCC to police may assist in remedying many of its recruitment issues.

title: Persistent Doors: Denial-Rate Stability and Structural Breaks Across Eleven of the Largest FHA Lenders, 2018-2025

detail.title: Persistent Doors: Denial-Rate Stability and Structural Breaks Across Eleven of the Largest FHA Lenders, 2018-2025
detail.abstract: A companion paper documents that in the 2025 HMDA record, lender identity accounts for 37.97 percent of all explained variation in FHA denial outcomes (Yetis, 2026). This paper asks whether that cross-sectional dispersion is durable structure or year-specific noise. Using an eight-year annual panel (2018-2025) of denial rates for eleven of the largest FHA lenders-88 lender-year cells built from the public HMDA record-I document three facts. First, the door hierarchy is nearly frozen: 80.8 percent of pooled variance in the panel is between lenders rather than within lenders over time, and the year-over-year Spearman rank correlation of lender orderings has a median of 0.918; the most lenient lender is the same institution in seven of eight years, and the runner-up is the same in seven of eight. Second, persistence is punctuated: count-based likelihood-ratio tests locate single regime shifts of at least five percentage points at four lenders-two large declines (-19.0 and-18.6 points) around 2019-2021 and two increases (+18.1 and +7.9 points) at the 2021-2022 rate-regime boundary. Third, only one lender exhibits a statistically significant monotone trend (Mann-Kendall p = 0.009; Sen slope-4.1 points per year). Because nearly any difference is statistically significant at these sample sizes, classification is by published magnitude thresholds, with test statistics reported for transparency. All estimates are associational; the series and code definitions are public under CC BY 4.0.

title: Prescriptive Analytics for Data-Driven Inventory Control: Introduction and Practical Research Opportunities
affiliations: Business Administration & Economics

detail.title: Prescriptive Analytics for Data-Driven Inventory Control: Introduction and Practical Research Opportunities
detail.abstract: Prescriptive analytics offers the opportunity to complement traditional inventory control methods with data-driven optimization approaches that leverage machine learning. This work reviews current applications of prescriptive analytics to inventory control from a practitioner's perspective and synthesizes findings from existing literature reviews and relevant studies. We identify three overarching practical limitations around the reflection of real-world problem complexity, the adaptation to real-world data regimes, and the flexibility in accommodating diverse problem settings. Building on these findings, we formulate two complementary research propositions: effectively using available data through cross-learning and effectively leveraging true state-of-the-art machine learning models across problems could further advance the benefits of data-driven optimization applied to real-world inventory control. Two numerical experiments demonstrate the potential of these propositions and provide empirical evidence that motivates future research in this direction.

title: Human, AI, and Organizational Performance (HAOP): A Safety Framework for the AI Era

detail.title: Human, AI, and Organizational Performance (HAOP): A Safety Framework for the AI Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author developed the HAOP framework and operates haop.ai, which provides related practitioner tools and materials. No other personal or financial relationships influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This work involved no research with human participants. Workplace incidents described are drawn from public regulatory records and published sources, or are presented anonymized at industry level.

detail.abstract:
Human, AI, and Organizational Performance (HAOP) is a safety framework that extends Human and Organizational Performance (HOP) to work systems in which AI performs consequential functions. It recognizes three performers within one work system: the human, who adapts; the AI, which optimizes within its representation and constraints; and the organization, which contains and governs, authoring the conditions under which the other two perform.

From this architecture, HAOP develops characteristic failure and contribution signatures and a five-hazard register for identifying hazards introduced or amplified by AI-enabled work. It adds five operating modes that classify how AI performs in the workflow; Accountability by Control, which keeps responsibility attached to the roles holding relevant control; and a work-design method organized by the industrial hygiene sequence of Anticipate, Recognize, Evaluate, Control, and Confirm (ARECC). The method specifies requirements for grounding; for human, automated, and hybrid Verification Gates; for Verification Capacity and Anchor Access; and for protected human pause authority and Designed AI Reassessment Pauses.

HAOP also introduces the AI Deployment Safety Data Sheet (ADSDS) as a bidirectional hazard-communication instrument, candidate leading measures for Verification Overrun as a prospective hazard condition, and the True Function Test as an initial diagnostic that organizations can apply now. The paper situates the framework alongside convergent 2026 work on delegated authority and designed oversight and examines insurance exclusions and assessment-based underwriting as emerging market demand for evidence of allocation, control, verification, and governance. HAOP and its integrated work-design method have not yet been empirically validated; the paper identifies a testing agenda for operational pilots and comparative evaluation.

title: The AI Dependency Index (IDA): Quantifying Minimum Workforce Continuity in AI-Dependent Organizations

detail.title: The AI Dependency Index (IDA): Quantifying Minimum Workforce Continuity in AI-Dependent Organizations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of All AIdeas SAS (Buenos Aires, Argentina), a consultancy working on artificial intelligence adoption, and teaches postgraduate and final-year project courses at Universidad Tecnologica Nacional, Facultad Regional Buenos Aires. detail.abstract: Problem. Organizations adopting artificial intelligence compute how many people they can release. We did not find a published framework that quantifies how many they must retain to keep operating if the provider becomes unavailable. Two developments in 2026 make that second number urgent: the price of inference is not anchored to any verifiable cost structure, and on 12 June 2026 a United States export-control order required a frontier provider to suspend two of its most advanced models for all foreign nationals; unable to verify nationality per user, the provider disabled both models for every customer worldwide until the controls were lifted on 30 June [5]. The disruption originated in policy, not infrastructure. Gap. Governance and operational-resilience frameworks prescribe dependency mapping, criticality tiering and fallback protocols. The AI Resilience Framework [1] extends impact-tolerance constructs to AI dependencies and identifies a quantitative substitutability score as an unrealised extension, which this work develops in workforce terms. Method. The AI Dependency Index (IDA) is a deterministic model built from six operational inputs managers already hold. It returns four outputs in one accounting: a retained workforce, a risk-adjusted saving, a maximum defensible investment, and a bounded 0-100 exposure score discounted by verified external backup. Findings. Past the continuity floor, further automation raises the AI bill without releasing anyone: savings fall while exposure rises. Under fixed-cost architectures savings plateau instead of falling, yet exposure still rises, so automation then buys dependency for nothing. Both behaviours follow from the equations. Availability. The model, its formulas, an executable implementation and a battery of 24 edge cases are published under the MIT licence and deposited with a permanent identifier [2]. It runs at modelo-ida.web.app.

title: Engaging Stakeholders as Research Collaborators: A Modern Blueprint for Workforce Development Research and Innovation

detail.abstract: This working paper presents a practical blueprint for engaging stakeholders as research collaborators in workforce development research and innovation. It argues that in complex organizational environments, research is most useful when those who influence, use, or are affected by findings participate throughout the research lifecycle. Drawing on stakeholder theory, evidence-based management, organizational development, participatory research, trust research, and change-management literature, the paper reframes stakeholder engagement as a strategic capability rather than a procedural activity. It outlines methods for identifying and prioritizing stakeholders, building trust, co-creating research agendas, sustaining engagement, tailoring participation strategies, and tracking engagement levels as indicators of organizational readiness and alignment. The paper emphasizes integrating stakeholder input with external research and internal data to create a contextual mosaic of evidence that improves decision quality and strengthens implementation. For workforce development practitioners, stakeholder engagement also functions as an intervention: it surfaces system dynamics, fosters psychological ownership, supports shared sensemaking, and accelerates adoption of research findings. The paper concludes that organizations that embed engagement into routine practice are better positioned to produce rigorous, relevant, actionable research while strengthening relationships, innovation capacity, and resilience.

title: Improving Intersection Safety Screening Through Probabilistic Severity Weighting
affiliations: Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University and Texas Tech University

detail.title: Improving Intersection Safety Screening Through Probabilistic Severity Weighting
detail.abstract: Annual intersection screening determines which locations enter safety evaluation when severe crashes are sparse and review budgets are limited. Severity weighted crash frequency gives agencies a traceable additive score, but each crash enters that score through a fixed severity class value. This study tests whether calibrated crash level probabilities of fatal or suspected serious injury can replace those fixed values without losing the audit structure of an additive site score. Crash Records Information System records from two Texas urban networks were processed through separate regional pipelines. Records were collapsed to the crash level, assigned deterministic intersection keys, screened for outcome leakage, modeled with balanced logistic regression, calibrated with sigmoid calibration using the last screening year, and aggregated to intersection scores. Scores from 2016 through 2021 crash histories were evaluated against fatal or suspected serious injury crashes observed from 2022 through 2025. At the 5% screening threshold, the probability weighted ranking captured 61 future severe crashes within the midsized network compared with 47 under fixed severity weighting, and 515 within the larger metropolitan network compared with 445. The same ordering held at the 10% and 15% thresholds. Probability weighted rankings also produced higher adjacent year Spearman rank stability in every evaluated base year. The evidence supports calibrated crash level probability as a consequence contribution for intersection network screening when calibration and leakage controls are maintained at the local data scale.

title: Data Science in Multi-Cloud Governance: Insights for Security, Scalability, and Risk Mitigation

detail.title: Data Science in Multi-Cloud Governance: Insights for Security, Scalability, and Risk Mitigation
detail.abstract: As companies search for more resilience, scalability, and flexibility in their IT systems, multi-cloud systems are becoming more and more used. Particularly with relation to security, scalability, and risk reduction, managing governance throughout several cloud platforms presents significant challenges. Conventional governance systems sometimes fall short in providing quick understanding of security concerns, compliance issues, and resource optimization. By use of advanced analytics, machine learning, and predictive modelling to translate raw multi-cloud data into actionable insights, data science offers a strong approach for addressing these challenges. Focusing especially on security, scalability, and risk management, this project aims to study how data science could help to improve governance in multi-cloud environments. Using a qualitative approach, the study incorporates secondary data drawn from reliable web databases spanning the years 2018 through 2024. Examining past studies, pointing up flaws in present governance systems, and assessing the effectiveness of data science approaches in multi-cloud governance was done by means of a comprehensive literature study. The findings showed that data-driven governance solutions greatly improve threat identification using anomaly detection models, distribute tasks optimally using predictive analytics, and lower compliance issues by automated monitoring systems. The paper emphasizes the need of robust data-driven governance systems and provides useful advice for project managers and decision-makers to improve security, scalability, and risk reducing methods in multi-cloud environments. New AI-driven governance models and the effect of automation on multi-cloud compliance management should be explored in next research projects. These results support the more general conversation on using data science for efficient cloud governance, hence promoting innovation and efficiency in multi-cloud systems.

title: Institutional Capital, PropTech, and the Spatial Dynamics of Housing Markets

detail.title: Institutional Capital, PropTech, and the Spatial Dynamics of Housing Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
