detail.abstract: A companion paper established, on the full record of World Bank evaluations, that the optimism bias of the economic rate of return grows with the ambition of the appraisal, and derived a reference-class deflation schedule from it. The present article tests that instrument on a named corridor, the Kankan–Kourémalé–Bamako road linking Guinea and Mali, whose appraisal we reconstruct from the African Development Bank report. We first reproduce exactly the appraisal rate of return of each of the two sections, 13.30 and 19.70 percent, from the published benefit stream, then decompose these benefits and set out the cost-benefit framework beneath them. We then apply the correction, which leaves the prudent section almost intact and heavily discounts the ambitious one. Three independent instruments, the margin after correction, the switching value and a Monte Carlo simulation, then converge on a counterintuitive result. The seemingly safest section, prudently appraised at 13.30 percent, is in fact the most fragile, with nearly a one-in-four chance of falling below the profitability hurdle, while the spectacular section, though heavily discounted, remains robust. A scenario analysis, a study of the sensitivity to traffic growth and to the discount rate, and a value-of-information reading of the verification count, sharpen the reach of the result. The lesson for appraisal practice is that a comfortable margin above the hurdle, once the bias is corrected, matters more than the announced level of the rate.

title: Centerline Rumble Strip Installation and Lane-Departure Crash Rates: A Segment-Year Before-After Analysis in Iowa
affiliations: Baum Tenpers Research

detail.title: Centerline Rumble Strip Installation and Lane-Departure Crash Rates: A Segment-Year Before-After Analysis in Iowa
detail.abstract: Centerline rumble strips are one of the roadway treatments commonly used to address lane-departure crashes, especially on rural roads where those crashes can be severe (Federal Highway Administration [FHWA], 2006, 2011, 2017; Torbic et al., 2009). This study used Iowa roadway and crash data with known installation year to examine whether lane-departure crash rates were lower after centerline rumble strip installation. Crash records were linked to roadway segments and arranged into a segment-year panel so that changes before and after treatment could be examined more directly. A comparison-group before-after negative binomial model was used to evaluate post-installation changes while accounting for exposure and selected roadway characteristics which is consistent with count-data practice in crash-frequency analysis (AASHTO, 2010; Lord & Mannering, 2010). In the adjusted model without speed grouping, the post-installation incidence rate ratio (IRR) was 0.640, which corresponds to about a 36.0% reduction in lane-departure crash rate. After grouped speed limit was added, the estimate remained very similar, with an IRR of 0.632, or about a 36.8% reduction. Event-time results also showed lower crash rates from the installation year onward. At the same time the years leading up to installation were not completely flat, so the findings are better interpreted as strong evidence consistent with effectiveness rather than final causal proof. Like in other studies (Persaud & Lyon, 2007), a full Empirical Bayes before-after evaluation would still provide the stronger causal framework for estimating treatment effect.

title: Does Food Assistance Drive Spending on Sugary Foods? Evidence from the Pandemic Electronic Benefit Transfer Program
affiliations: American University and American University

detail.title: Does Food Assistance Drive Spending on Sugary Foods? Evidence from the Pandemic Electronic Benefit Transfer Program

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: All phases of this study were supported by a National Institutes of Health (NIH) grant, R01DK140192 (PI: Brandyn Churchill). The views expressed herein are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the NIH. The NIH had no role in the design or conduct of the study.

detail.abstract: Although it is unclear whether food assistance contributes to lower diet quality among recipients, policymakers are actively working to restrict SNAP-eligible purchases of items high in added sugars. We provide timely evidence on the extent to which food assistance increases spending on sugary items by studying the Pandemic Electronic Benefit Transfer (P-EBT) program, which provided food assistance benefits to families of children who lost access to free and reduced-price school meals due to COVID-19 pandemic school closures. Leveraging state-level variation in the timing of P-EBT disbursements and using a stacked difference-indifferences identification strategy with NielsenIQ Consumer Panel data, we find that P-EBT disbursement was associated with a 16-percent increase in weekly spending on sugary items among SNAP-eligible households with school-aged children. Notably, this increase exceeded the percentage increase in overall food spending for this group, suggesting that SNAP-eligible households with school-aged children allocated a disproportionately large share of their P-EBT-driven purchases toward sugary items relative to their pre-period baseline. We do not detect changes among households unlikely to have received P-EBT benefits or in placebo disbursement years.

title: Modeling the Economic & Political Determinants of Chinese FDI in Africa

detail.title: Modeling the Economic & Political Determinants of Chinese FDI in Africa
detail.abstract: This paper contributes to the burgeoning literature regarding China’s increased engagement in the developing world, specifically in Africa, where the PRC has historically sought strong diplomatic ties. This study aims to evaluate the characteristics of African countries that dictate the distribution of Chinese Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) across the continent. To estimate the determinants of Chinese FDI across Africa, a two-way fixed effects model is used, which allows the effects of common FDI determinants like GDP, trade openness, and institutional quality to be isolated while controlling for country-specific and time-specific variation. This model contributes to the existing literature on Chinese FDI in Africa by offering an analysis of the key determinants of Chinese FDI on a continental scale, as well as addressing why heterogeneous effects of key determinants are often observed within the literature. To ensure the validity of results, a number of robustness tests are performed. This includes a Wald test for heteroskedasticity, an investigation of potential multicollinearity among independent variables using the variance inflation factor (VIF), and a series of Im-Pesaran-Shin tests for stationarity to determine whether independent variable characteristics change in the long run. The multiple models and ensuing analysis yield multiple interesting results. Primarily, it is found that Chinese FDI Stock in a given country is closely related to GDP and, therefore, market size. It is also found that China's FDI Stock is positively related to an index cataloging a given country’s political and institutional characteristics, and is negatively related to a country’s trade openness. The findings of this study provide important insights for African governments seeking to navigate the rise of China’s engagement on the continent, and also challenge the traditional narrative of exploitative Chinese investment in Africa.

title: AI Adoption and Stock Return Dynamics in Indian Banking: Evidence from Public and Private Sector Banks
affiliations: Acharya Institute of Graduate Studies, Acharya Institute of Graduate Studies and Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Open University

detail.title: AI Adoption and Stock Return Dynamics in Indian Banking: Evidence from Public and Private Sector Banks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest and no personal or financial relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses secondary, publicly available data (annual reports, financial statements, and stock market data) and does not involve human participants or patient data; therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agency.

detail.abstract: While Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming financial intermediation, its impact on equity valuation, particularly within emerging economies such as India, remains opaque. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and stock return dynamics in Indian banking using a balanced panel of ten major listed Indian banks, divided equally between public and private sector banks from fiscal year 2011-2025. Employing two-way fixed effects models, we evaluate whether AI integration, operationalized via binary indicator and a continuous intensity index, explains the variations in stock returns after controlling for bank-specific financial fundamentals and idiosyncratic risk. Under standard clustered standard errors, AI adoption shows no statistically significant effect on abnormal returns; however, under wild cluster bootstrap inference (more appropriate given the small number of cross-sectional clusters), the AI adoption coefficient is negative and economically borderline at the 5 percent level. The results remain consistent across ownership-interaction models, placebo tests, and dynamic event-time specifications. Adjacent to return-based findings, AI adoption shows no significant association with Return on Assets (ROA), a key profitability metric for Indian banking stocks. This could possibly be explained by a potential increase in operational costs associated with adoption and integration of AI technologies which offsets the productivity gains, leading to a productivity paradox. Altogether, the findings suggest that capital markets do not immediately reward, and may marginally penalize digital transformation initiatives in the Indian banking sector in the short run, consistent with investor scepticism about the near-term productivity gains or the internalization of implementation costs.

title: In Situ Structural Transformation and Women's Autonomy: Evidence from Rural Bangladesh
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: In Situ Structural Transformation and Women's Autonomy: Evidence from Rural Bangladesh
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how in situ structural transformation, where men transition out of agriculture but remain in their communities, affects norm-based restrictions on women's autonomy. Using panel data from rural Bangladesh and a Double/Debiased Machine Learning approach, I isolate the effect of male occupational transitions on six indicators of female seclusion. I develop a theoretical framework modeling these restrictions as an equilibrium between the income-driven demand for patriarchal status and the rising efficiency costs of enforcement. Empirically, I find modest and statistically insignificant aggregate relaxations across most restrictions. However, these averages mask substantial heterogeneity: restrictions tighten among small landholding households but relax significantly for wealthier households, with effects also varying by household gender composition. Ultimately, male-biased economic shocks do not uniformly liberalize or tighten gender norms. Instead, changes depend on the specific enforcement costs and status-generating properties of individual restrictions.

title: Geospatial Imagery and Machine Learning in Commercial Real Estate Valuation
affiliations: University of Central Florida, Auburn University - Department of Finance, Florida State University and University of South Florida

detail.title: Geospatial Imagery and Machine Learning in Commercial Real Estate Valuation
detail.abstract: Investors price commercial property partly on how it looks, yet visual attributes rarely appear in the data used to study transaction pricing. Using satellite and street view imagery for 6,533 U.S. single-tenant net lease transactions from 2005 to 2020, we read each property's images two ways: as scores against attributes we name in advance, and as unlabeled statistical summaries. Together they close about 6.5 percent of the cap rate variation left unexplained by conventional property, market, lease, and time controls, and the named attributes account for most of it. The gain survives county fixed effects, public controls for walkability, demographics, urban form, and flood risk, and it improves out-of-sample forecasts. Because most of what imagery contributes can be stated in words, appraisal and underwriting can use it without sacrificing transparency.

title: Sampford Apportionment Satisfies Threshold Monotonicity
affiliations: , University of New South Wales (UNSW) and University of New South Wales (UNSW)

detail.title: Sampford Apportionment Satisfies Threshold Monotonicity

declarations.funderStatement: Haris Aziz and Simon Mackenzie are supported by the NSF-CSIRO grant on “Fair Sequential Collective Decision-Making” (RG230833). Mashbat Suzuki is supported by the ARC Laureate Project FL200100204 on “Trustworthy AI”.

detail.abstract: Apportionment distributes a fixed number of legislative seats among political parties in proportion to their vote shares. Randomization can satisfy quota in every realization and exact proportionality in expectation, but these requirements determine only the parties' marginal seat distributions. We study threshold monotonicity, which requires that when every standard quota inside a coalition weakly increases and every standard quota outside it weakly decreases, the coalition's new seat total stochastically dominates its old one. We prove that Sampford apportionment satisfies threshold monotonicity, resolving the threshold-monotonicity conjecture of Correa et al. (2024). Complementing this result, we prove that no quota-respecting, ex-ante proportional method satisfies pairwise threshold monotonicity even for disjoint coalitions when there are at least seven parties. This impossibility applies whether or not the method has full support.

title: The Substance Trap Transfer Pricing and the Global Minimum Tax After the 2026 Side by Side Package: Long Run Consequences for West Africa and for Nigeria

detail.title: The Substance Trap Transfer Pricing and the Global Minimum Tax After the 2026 Side by Side Package: Long Run Consequences for West Africa and for Nigeria
detail.abstract: The international tax settlement changed shape twice in eighteen months. In June 2025 Nigeria enacted a domestic minimum effective tax rate of fifteen percent, effective January 2026, and in January 2026 the Inclusive Framework agreed a Side by Side package that exempts United States parented groups from the two principal charging rules of the global minimum tax and introduces a Substance based Tax Incentive Safe Harbour. I argue that the second of these changes carries a distributional consequence for low wage economies that has not been priced into African policy debate. The safe harbour protects a tax incentive only up to a cap set at five and a half percent of eligible payroll costs, so the fraction of an incentive that survives is proportional to the wage bill a jurisdiction happens to carry per unit of taxable profit. I show that a full exemption is preserved intact only where payroll exceeds GloBE income by a factor of 2.73, a threshold no plausible West African configuration reaches, while an economy with an OECD style labour share sits within reach of it. The minimum tax is therefore not neutral across development levels: it is neutral in wages, which is a different and much less attractive property. Three implications follow. Regionally, tax holidays have become a transfer from West African treasuries to foreign ones, and the only reliable instrument of recapture is a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax, which no Economic Community of West African States member has yet enacted. Nationally, Nigeria's section 57 rule is close to that instrument but not identical to it, and I show that whenever GloBE income exceeds the Nigerian statutory base by a factor δ, a residual foreign claim of τ (1-1/δ) survives full domestic compliance, worth three percentage points of profit at δ = 1.25 and five at δ = 1.50. The reform priority is base alignment and qualification, not rate setting.

title: The Digital Sovereignty Trap: Fragmentation, Retaliation and the Limits of Regulatory Power

detail.title: The Digital Sovereignty Trap: Fragmentation, Retaliation and the Limits of Regulatory Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an official of the European Commission, representing the EU on digital policy issues in G20, G7 and trade negotiations, and teaches International Digital Policies and Regulations at Sciences-Po Paris.

contentType.other: Revised manuscript, submitted to Computer Law & Security Review — currently under peer review after first round of reviewer comments (manuscript CLSR-D-26-00799).

detail.abstract: "Digital sovereignty" is one of the most invoked yet least legally defined concepts in contemporary regulatory discourse. For example, across eight major jurisdictions (the European Union, the United States, China, the United Kingdom (UK), India, Brazil, Canada and Japan) governments are putting digital sovereignty at the top of their agenda, appointing ministers responsible for it, enacting measures justified by appeals to this objective, yet the legal content of that concept varies dramatically by actor, by layer of the digital stack targeted, and by the underlying justification advanced. This article argues that digital sovereignty is not yet a coherent legal principle, but a contested political claim translated into fragmented regulatory instruments. Through a comparative analysis of legislative design and enforcement mechanisms, the article develops, building on prior scholarship in digital policy studies, a typology of four archetypes of sovereignty claims (data sovereignty, technological sovereignty, regulatory sovereignty, and jurisdictional sovereignty) and maps how each is being operationalised. It then examines a paradox: the stronger the assertion of digital sovereignty, the more it provokes counter-assertions by others, progressively eroding the sovereignty of all. Drawing on WTO law, trade agreements, and emerging international coalitions, the article proposes possible legal avenues for distinguishing legitimate digital sovereignty claims from disguised protectionism, and concludes that, absent multilateral discipline, the current fragmentation risks producing a sovereignty trap from which no actor can escape.

title: On Tuberculosis Incidence, Health Expenditure and the Macroeconomy:,Insights from Cross- Country Data
affiliations: Monash University - Monash University Malaysia, University of the Philippines Diliman and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: On Tuberculosis Incidence, Health Expenditure and the Macroeconomy:,Insights from Cross- Country Data
detail.abstract: This study examines the determinants of tuberculosis (TB) incidence using a Poisson spatial autoregressive model that incorporates macroeconomic, socioeconomic, population health, and public health expenditure indicators. Spatial dependence is captured through a spatial autoregressive component based on average per capita health expenditure within income regions. Using pooled cross-country data, parameters are estimated through a backfitting algorithm combining conditional least squares and maximum likelihood estimation, while statistical significance is evaluated using the AR Sieve Bootstrap.,Results show that the inclusion of both temporal and spatial autoregressive effects improves the predictive performance of conventional Poisson regression models. TB incidence is significantly influenced by socioeconomic conditions, underscoring the role of social and economic factors in shaping disease burden. A positive and significant spatial effect is also observed, suggesting that public health expenditures within an income region influence health outcomes, including TB incidence.,The findings highlight the importance of sustained government investment in public health programs for controlling communicable diseases. Equally important is the strategic allocation of health resources toward interventions that address disease transmission and socioeconomic vulnerabilities. Targeted, pro-poor health policies that promote equitable access to healthcare can reduce the financial burden on affected households and improve population health outcomes. Overall, the results support prioritizing health expenditures that simultaneously address the social determinants of health and communicable disease control.

title: The Value of Tax Transparency
affiliations: University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business, University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business and

detail.title: The Value of Tax Transparency
detail.abstract: We examine investor responses to the first jurisdiction-level income tax disclosures required under new accounting standards (ASU 2023-09). Using firms' first ASU 2023-09 compliant Form 10-K filings, we find that firms experience significantly more favorable filing window abnormal returns, ranging from 1.4 to 1.6 percentage points, when the expanded effective tax rate reconciliation reveals that any foreign jurisdiction materially lowers the firm's effective tax rate. This reaction is concentrated among tax havens. A complementary intensive-margin test, using the number of haven jurisdictions a firm discloses rather than a binary indicator, corroborates this concentration: the market reaction rises significantly with each additional haven jurisdiction disclosed. Overall, our findings provide initial evidence that investors value the enhanced transparency introduced by new tax disclosure requirements, particularly information conveyed through the expanded effective tax rate reconciliation, and that this value is concentrated in disclosures identifying economically significant tax-haven activity.

title: The Singleton Effect: Isolated Digits Overturn the Presumed Hierarchy of Cultural Number Preferences

detail.title: The Singleton Effect: Isolated Digits Overturn the Presumed Hierarchy of Cultural Number Preferences

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available, non-human-subject archival data (lottery draw and payout records) and does not require ethics committee approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: A substantial literature documents that culturally lucky numbers shape economic behavior, from stock listing codes to housing prices to trading decisions, with the digit 8-associated with wealth in Chinese culture-consistently identified as the dominant cultural anchor. We show this consensus reflects a measurement artifact: prior studies measure preference through multi-digit identifiers (stock tickers, addresses, license plates), conflating positional salience with the strength of a digit's underlying cultural meaning. Using 24 years of data from the Hong Kong Mark Six lottery-3,277 draws and over US$20 billion in turnover-we exploit a discontinuity between prize tiers that isolates a single digit from combinatorial noise. First, contrary to the presumed hierarchy, digit 9 is selected 37% more often than chance, exceeding 8's 27% premium. Second, the "Singleton Effect" explains why: digit 9's pull collapses nearly 90% once embedded in a compound identifier, versus only 38% for 8, explaining why decades of compound-identifier-based studies converged on the wrong anchor. Third, we quantify the economic cost of this preference at the singleton level, free of the compound-identifier contamination affecting many prior premium estimates: digit 9 commands an "Auspiciousness Premium" of 18.6%, versus 16.3% for digit 8, while the culturally shunned 40s range earns a "Tetraphobia Discount" of up to 23.3%. Together, our findings offer a template for isolating the true magnitude of willingness to pay for cultural preferences wherever compound identifiers may dilute existing estimates.

title: Learning, No-Arbitrage and the Term Structure of Equity Risk Premia
affiliations: University of Leicester - School of Business

detail.title: Learning, No-Arbitrage and the Term Structure of Equity Risk Premia
detail.abstract: This paper develops a learning-based explanation for the term structure of equity risk premia. Investors have rational beliefs about consumption and dividends but learn from stock prices about future risk-adjusted capital gains. These subjective price beliefs affect the aggregate stock and stock-futures prices. No-arbitrage then transmits the resulting belief wedge into dividend-futures prices, even though investors correctly understand dividend fundamentals. Because this transmission strengthens with maturity, long-maturity dividend claims become increasingly exposed to aggregate market risk. The model generates declining Sharpe ratios, rising CAPM betas, positive short-horizon alphas, and countercyclical equity term premia. Simulations and dividend-futures evidence support these predictions.

title: Canopeo-derived fractional green canopy cover as a rapid, non-destructive endpoint for contact herbicide efficacy assessment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Canopeo-derived fractional green canopy cover as a rapid, non-destructive endpoint for contact herbicide efficacy assessment
detail.abstract: The development of new herbicidal products requires robust, reproducible, and practical methods for evaluating efficacy. However, reliable assessment of herbicide efficacy remains challenging because conventional visual evaluation is subjective and difficult to standardize, whereas biomass measurement is destructive and unsuitable for repeated assessment. This study evaluated Canopeo-derived fractional green canopy cover (FGCC) from RGB images as a rapid, non-destructive proxy for biomass-based assessment of contact herbicide efficacy under controlled conditions. Two morphologically contrasting plant models were selected: the monocot Lolium perenne and the dicot Arabidopsis thaliana. After evaluating three image-acquisition angles in L. perenne (lateral, oblique, and nadir) and identifying the lateral view as the most suitable, the FGCC-based method and visual injury assessment were compared with biomass reduction in both species. FGCC and biomass reduction showed close numerical agreement in L. perenne (R² = 0.981, CCC = 0.990) and A. thaliana (R² = 0.986, CCC = 0.982), whereas visual assessment showed lower concordance and greater dispersion, particularly in L. perenne. Overall, Canopeo-derived FGCC appears to provide a rapid, affordable, and standardized endpoint for contact herbicide efficacy trials.

title: The Frozen Cohort: Assessment Caps, Historical Credit Geography, and the Inheritance of Tax Advantage in Los Angeles

detail.title: The Frozen Cohort: Assessment Caps, Historical Credit Geography, and the Inheritance of Tax Advantage in Los Angeles

detail.abstract: Proposition 13 ties a California property's tax to its value at acquisition, so the year a household entered ownership sets its tax rate indefinitely. We measure the resulting subsidy across the universe of Los Angeles City residential parcels (N = 694,441), using exact per-parcel tax rates and a valuation model calibrated on held-out sales. The subsidy totals $4.6 to $6.8 billion per year and follows a perfectly monotonic acquisition-cohort gradient: pre-1979 basis holders pay an effective rate of 0.100 percent of market value; buyers at current prices pay 1.000 percent. The subsidy is not an owner-occupant program; landlord-held parcels carry larger median subsidies in every cohort holding material subsidy. It is ordered by the 1939 Home Owners' Loan Corporation grades, but a boundary discontinuity test with certified shared borders and clustered inference shows the gaps collapse at grade lines, supporting incidence along historical valuation geography rather than a causal line effect. Archival census tabulations anchor the advantaged cohort's formation: in 1970, women headed 8.0 percent of the county's multi-person owner households and 14.2 percent of its renter households. Finally, using the assessor's own reappraisal adjudications, we measure the subsidy's inheritance directly. Among pre-1979-basis parcels, 22.1 percent carry a completed parent-child exclusion claim and 85.5 percent sit within the estate-planning apparatus. Together these place $770 million of the cohort's $924 million annual subsidy on basis that has already crossed a generation or entered the machinery that carries it. The advantage the old credit regime rationed is now, in substantial part, an inheritance.

title: Calibration in Prediction Markets: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: Kalshi and

detail.title: Calibration in Prediction Markets: Theory and Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Both authors are employed by Kalshi Inc., the prediction market exchange whose data is analyzed in this paper. The study uses proprietary Kalshi datasets in addition to publicly available API data. The authors received no compensation contingent on the findings reported here, and Kalshi Inc. placed no restrictions on the analysis or its conclusions.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was part of the authors' employment. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: Prediction markets are commonly described as producing prices that admit a literal probabilistic interpretation, but this empirical claim has yet to be evaluated at scale on any U.S.-regulated exchange. This paper represents the first such exercise, using the complete history of resolved markets on Kalshi-the world's largest prediction market-comprising 2,243,741 markets across eleven categories from the platform's launch in 2021 through mid-2026, to evaluate calibration and accuracy as functions of time-to-resolution, trading volume, and the number of participating traders. We document that Kalshi's prices are, in aggregate, extremely well calibrated as markets approach resolution. Assessing all markets (excluding Exotics), we record a decline in Brier score from approximately 0.08-0.09 at a 3-Month horizon to roughly 0.02 at Close. Further, reliability diagrams track the 45°line closely across nearly every category examined. In parallel, we note that naive accuracy rises from 88.3% at a 3-Month horizon to 97.2% at Close. Beneath these strong aggregate results lie more granular conclusions. First, calibration quality improves nearmonotonically with both event-level trading volume and the number of unique traders, which we interpret as preliminary evidence that deeper participation may sharpen prices rather than distort them. Second, calibration is stronger and accuracy higher for high-attention categories listed well in advance, such as Economics, than for categories for which the information discovery period is limited and outcomes widely dispersed, such as Mentions. Third, though it is a natural assumption that calibration is a linear function of time-to-resolution, we find that anchoring to the true timing of the underlying event's occurrence rather than to raw closing timestamps, which may be subject to significant delay, unexpectedly improves calibration in Sports and de-biases results in Elections. To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to re-scale expiration times in the study of prediction markets. We interpret these findings, taken together, as variation around a strong baseline rather than as a qualification of it: Kalshi's prices behave like genuine probabilities, and increasingly so as resolution approaches.

title: Occupational Mobility Is Not One Thing: Evidence from the Canadian Labour Market

detail.title: Occupational Mobility Is Not One Thing: Evidence from the Canadian Labour Market

declarations.funderStatement: Government of British Columbia

detail.abstract: Education-occupation pipelines sort workers into occupations by specificity, and how specific an occupation a worker lands in governs which geometry rules their subsequent moves. Using entropic regularized optimal transport, we run a horse race among three distance metrics and find that no single geometry governs local mobility: the metric depends on an occupation's education specificity, skill where human capital is general, hierarchy where intermediate, binary where so occupation-specific that neither predicts destinations. The specificity that governs local mobility is thus endogenous, set by the pipeline that previously placed the worker. Each regime implies a distinct policy lever for labour shortages.
